sens: to reduce to fragments, to break an object
to shatter, to fragment a group
to disperse, to scatter a community
H8600.detail:
1. To break literally means to reduce something to pieces, like breaking a fragile object. In Jeremiah 25:34, the image is that of a precious pottery being shattered: "I will break you, and you will fall like a priceless vase." 
2. The word also applies to fragmenting or breaking a group into separate parts, which leads to its destruction or weakening. 
3. By extension, to break can mean to disperse, to scatter a community or a people in different directions, separating them from one another. This is what happens to the shepherds and leaders that God threatens with fragmentation.
H8600.origine: The Hebrew word תְּפוֹצָה (tephoutsa) comes from the root פּוּץ (poutz), which means "to disperse, to scatter." This root expresses the idea of distributing in all directions, of breaking into pieces. The noun תְּפוֹצָה thus denotes the action or result of this dispersion — either the breaking into pieces or the scattering of a community.
H8600.emploi: This word appears only once in the Bible, in Jeremiah 25:34. In this passage, God addresses the shepherds and leaders of Israel and announces a terrible punishment: they will be broken, fragmented like a precious vase that shatters. The prophetic context shows that this breaking is not only physical but also symbolic — it represents the destruction of leadership and the dispersion of the people.
H8600.portee: This word reminds the believer that God is sovereign over the powerful of this world. It teaches that breaking and dispersion can be divine judgment on those who have failed in their responsibility as shepherds and guides. For the reader, it is an invitation to examine their own faithfulness to God and to those they have been entrusted to protect.

sens: Fragment of bread or cake baked in the oven
Part of a cooked grain offering
H8601.detail: 1. The word designates a piece or fragment of cooked food, probably bread or a cake. It is the image of a solid piece, broken or divided, taken out of the fire. 2. In the context of Israelite worship, it refers to pieces of a grain offering (minḥa) that have been baked in the oven and then fragmented. In Leviticus 6:14, the priest must eat "a piece of this offering" presented to the Lord — which shows that the shared sacrifice included concrete, tangible portions intended for ritual consumption.
H8601.origine: The word comes from a Hebrew root meaning "to break" or "to shatter." It literally describes what has been broken or fragmented. The plural suffix indicates several pieces. This rare form reflects the technical vocabulary of temple worship, where every detail of the offerings was meticulously regulated.
H8601.emploi: The word appears only once in the Hebrew Bible, in Leviticus 6:14, in the laws concerning the grain offering (minḥa). It describes the portions that the priest was to consume from the sacrifice that was not entirely burned. This cultic context suggests a technical, precise meaning related to temple practices. The unique occurrence and uncertain definition indicate that it is a specialized term from sacrificial vocabulary.
H8601.portee: This word reminds us that Israel's worship was not abstract: it involved concrete actions, shared meals between God and His priests. The baked pieces symbolize the tangible reality of serving God and the communion established through sacrifice.

sens: That has no taste, that is flavorless
That lacks strength or substance, that is vain or hollow
That is false, deceptive, without foundation
H8602A.detail:
1. In the literal sense, what has no taste: egg white is bland, meaning it has no pleasant flavor (Job 6:6). The image is that of food that disappoints, that does not truly nourish the palate. 
2. In a figurative sense, what lacks weight, value, or truth: the visions that the false prophets give to Jerusalem are bland, vain, and empty of reality (Lamentations 2:14). They claim to comfort, but they say nothing that corresponds to the truth. 
3. More specifically, what is false and deceptive: these bland visions are also called lies and deceptive oracles (Lamentations 2:14), as they hide sin instead of revealing it.
H8602A.origine: The Hebrew תָּפֵל (taphel) primarily denotes the absence of flavor. It is a concrete word that evokes tasteless food, without salt or seasoning. The absence of taste naturally becomes the image of what lacks substance, truth, or strength.
H8602A.emploi: The word appears only twice in the Hebrew Bible. In Job 6:6, it describes the egg white, a tasteless food that Job refuses to eat as his illness has disgusted him even of bland things. In Lamentations 2:14, applied to the prophets, it qualifies their vain and false visions — these prophets of besieged Jerusalem give deceptive oracles instead of calling the people to repentance. In both contexts, the word carries a connotation of disappointment: there is nothing nourishing, nothing true to expect from it.
H8602A.portee: This word invites the believer to discern: beware of hollow words, unfounded prophecies, cheap consolations. They may seem flattering or comforting, but they are bland — without substance, without truth. The true spiritual food is the Word of God that speaks the truth, even when it is difficult to hear, even when it calls for repentance rather than illusion.

sens: White or light coating applied to a wall to cover or decorate it
Mask or deceptive appearance that hides weakness or lies
Lying words presented as a message from God
H8602B.detail:
1. Plaster is literally a white substance that is applied to a wall to cover it. In Ezekiel's vision, the lying prophets cover the breaches of a bad wall with plaster: the coating masks instability, but when the rain and hail come, everything will collapse (Ezekiel 13:10-15). 
2. Plaster becomes the image of a deceptive appearance: something that shines on the surface but does not stand firm. The false prophets use "plaster" — coatings, flattering words — to hide reality and seduce the people. 
3. More broadly, plaster symbolizes prophetic falsehood: lies presented as the word of the Lord. In Ezekiel 22:28, the prophets have "plaster coatings," that is, vain visions and lying oracles.
H8602B.origine: The Hebrew word תָּפֵל (taphel) comes from a root meaning to spread or apply a coating. It specifically denotes plaster or a white coating used to conceal the defects of a construction. The image is that of something ephemeral added to the surface: neither solid, nor durable, nor true.
H8602B.emploi: This word appears only five times in biblical Hebrew, all in the book of Ezekiel, in chapters 13 and 22. Ezekiel uses it to describe the work of false prophets who reassure the people by saying "Peace!" when there is no peace (13:10). They "cover with plaster" a poorly constructed wall, in other words, they present false assurances about the spiritual solidity of Israel. In 22:28, plaster becomes an image of vain visions and lying oracles: the false prophets work for those who pay them, coating their lies with a divine appearance.
H8602B.portee: This word teaches the Christian to be wary of what shines on the surface without a solid foundation. False prophets, yesterday as today, coat their lies with an appearance of spirituality. Ezekiel's plaster reminds us that the true word of God does not flatter: it warns, it calls for conversion, and it stands firm when everything collapses. Seeking the truth means looking at the foundations, not the coatings.

sens: Desert place located southeast of the Dead Sea, in or near the Arabah
H8603.detail: Tophel is a location in the southeastern Arabian desert, mentioned only once in the Bible as a geographical landmark when Moses delivers his farewell address to Israel. The name literally means "white" in Hebrew, likely referring to the color of the soil or rocks in this arid region. Although its exact location is not known with certainty today, it was situated between the Dead Sea and the Gulf of Aqaba, in the region called the Arabah, a large desert depression that extends from the south of the Sea of Galilee to the Red Sea (Deuteronomy 1:1).
H8603.origine: The Hebrew word תֹּ֫פֶל (Tophel) comes from a root meaning "white" or "pale." This descriptive name reflects the appearance of the desert landscape in this region, where white or whitish rocks are characteristic. No other occurrence of the word appears in the Bible, making it a place mentioned only once in the sacred text.
H8603.emploi: Tophel appears only once in the Bible, in Deuteronomy 1:1, where it is listed among several locations serving as landmarks to indicate where Moses delivered his final words to Israel before entering the Promised Land. It is mentioned between Paran and Laban in a list of desert locations, emphasizing that this foundational speech was given not in the Promised Land, but in the desert, reminding the Israelites that this last exhortation from the great legislator reached them in the desert of the Arabah.

sens: That which is empty of meaning, lacking foundation
Action or word that contradicts the natural or moral order
Behavior or act that is rebellious, lacking wisdom or justice
H8604.detail:
1. The word first evokes something hollow and devoid of substance: an empty word, an inconsistent thought. It is folly in the sense of absence of reason. When Job refuses to attribute anything "unjust" to God (Job 1:22), he refuses to fall into this void, this thought that has no grip on reality.
2. The word also designates what is indecent, inappropriate on a moral level — an action that violates the established order, that shocks. Thus, in Job 24:12, the "infamies" are the cries of distress from victims, acts that offend the decency and justice that God should uphold.
3. By extension, it is the senseless act, the rebellion of one who ignores wisdom or refuses to listen to it. The prophets of Samaria who prophesy by Baal commit "extravagance" (Jeremiah 23:13): they do what is foolish, dangerous, far from the truth of God.
H8604.origine: The Hebrew word comes from a root that suggests the idea of what is hollow, light, without substance. The family of this word in Hebrew regularly expresses what is devoid of weight, foundation, or moral value. In Greek, this notion is close to folly (ἄνοια) — not a mental illness, but the absence of meaning, voluntary wandering.
H8604.emploi: The word appears only three times in biblical Hebrew, always among the wise and in Jeremiah. In Job 1:22, it expresses the refusal to say or think a folly against God — a protection of the soul. In Job 24:12, it designates indignity, glaring injustice. In Jeremiah 23:13, it qualifies false prophecy, the word that leads Israel away from the path of God. Each time, the context shows that this folly is a peril: it distances from the truth, it offends, it misleads.
H8604.portee: This word reminds the reader of the difference between true wisdom and folly. For a believer, it is about not falling back into the foolishness of blaming God or attributing injustice to Him (Job 1:22); not ignoring the cries of victims (Job 24:12); and discerning false prophets, those who speak in the name of a deity other than the true God (Jeremiah 23:13). Rejecting folly is choosing clarity and attentiveness.

sens: Request addressed to God with respect and trust
Words by which one expresses needs or gratitude before the Lord
Religious act of communion with God
Attitude of the heart that turns to God
H8605.detail:
1. Prayer is primarily a request addressed to God with respect and trust: this is what David expresses when he says, "I will build you a house! That is why your servant has taken courage to address this prayer to you" (2 Samuel 7:27), showing how one approaches God to make known their wishes.
2. It is also the set of words by which one expresses their needs, pains, or gratitude: the Psalmist cries, "Hear my cries, be attentive to my prayer!" (Psalms 61:2), showing that prayer puts into words what weighs on the heart.
3. Prayer is a religious act, a form of worship by which one presents themselves before God: this is why the Temple is called "house of prayer" (Isaiah 56:7), a place dedicated to this encounter.
4. It is also an attitude of the heart that turns to God with sincerity: "the prayer of the upright is pleasing to Him" (Proverbs 15:8) teaches that God listens especially to those who pray with integrity.
H8605.origine: The word comes from a root that means "to judge, examine, discern": prayer is the moment when one examines themselves before God and seeks His judgment or opinion. This is also why this word designates the act of praying itself. In Hebrew, it is a concrete feminine noun that designates both the act and its result — the spoken words. The word appears mainly in the Psalms and Lamentations, where it is often at the heart of the Temple liturgy.
H8605.emploi: This word appears 71 times in the Old Testament, primarily in the Psalms (over 30 occurrences), in Kings and Chronicles (where the prayer of the Temple is discussed), and in the prophets. David, Nehemiah, and Isaiah use it to refer to their requests to God. Very often, expressions like "God hears the prayer" (Psalms 66:19) or "the prayer rises to God" (Psalms 88:14) are found, showing that prayer is the intermediary between man and heaven. The word can refer to both intercessory prayer and thanksgiving. Its use reveals that for the people of Israel, prayer is not a spiritual luxury, but the primary weapon and fundamental duty of the believer.
H8605.portee: This word reminds the reader that access to God is direct and open: no magical ritual, no mandatory intermediary, but a sincere word addressed to the Father. Learning this word is to understand that prayer — a simple request of the heart — is the spiritual breath of the believer. It is also to discover that God pays real attention to those who pray to Him with righteousness, and that prayer is never in vain when it comes from a heart turned toward Him.

sens: Excessive pride, overconfidence in oneself
Arrogant assurance that blinds and misleads
Foolish confidence in one's own strength or position
H8606.detail:
1. Presumption is primarily an exaggerated confidence in oneself, a pride that leads someone to believe they are above others or invulnerable. In the passage from Jeremiah 49:16, the Edomite imagines himself impregnable because he dwells in "the clefts of the rocks," at the top of the hills: his geographical position gives him the illusion that he can challenge even God.

2. This presumption is all the more dangerous as it misleads those who allow themselves to be filled with it: it diverts them from the right path by giving them a false vision of their importance and security. It is a form of moral blindness.

3. The word also carries a nuance of trembling or terrified fear directed towards oneself — this noisy assurance of the presumptuous person who actually hides an inner fragility and a panic in the face of what might disturb them.
H8606.origine: The word comes from a Hebrew root that evokes the idea of a jolt, a shiver, an involuntary contraction of fear. But here, this initial shiver has transformed into a feeling of boastful pride: it is the presumption of the small man who secretly trembles but shouts loudly to avoid admitting it. The morphology of the word also suggests a form of inner panic, an agitation that the presumptuous person seeks to mask with their arrogance.
H8606.emploi: The word appears only once in the Bible, in Jeremiah 49:16, in an oracle against Edom. The Edomite is so blinded by the presumption inspired by his naturally fortified position in the rocks that he does not see God's judgment approaching. This presumption is not merely a psychological trait: it is a sin, a rebellion against God, a self-confidence that refuses to acknowledge its dependence on the Creator. The Lord promises precisely to bring this presumptuous one down from his height, showing that God does not tolerate human arrogance.
H8606.portee: Presumption is a major spiritual danger in the Christian faith. This text warns the believer not to rely on their own strengths or apparent securities — wealth, power, position — as if they shielded them from God's judgment. True wisdom lies in humility and recognition of divine sovereignty, not in the pride that blinds and precedes a fall.

sens: City on the northeastern border of Solomon's empire, on the Euphrates
H8607G.detail: Thiphsach is an important city located at the northeastern limit of the territory conquered by Solomon, on the banks of the Euphrates. Its name literally means "to pass" or "to cross" in Hebrew, evoking the crossing of the river. It marks the extreme border of the empire to the northeast, symbolizing the extent of Solomon's power which ruled "over all the land on the other side of the river, from Thiphsach to Gaza" (1 Kings 4:24).
H8607G.origine: The Hebrew name תִּפְסַח (tiph'sach) comes from the root פסח (psach) which means "to pass" or "to cross." This etymology reflects the geographical position of the city: it stands on the Euphrates, a river that must be crossed to access the northeastern territories. The name thus evokes the idea of a passage or transition, which was perfectly suited to a border city of the empire.
H8607G.emploi: Thiphsach appears only once in the Bible, in 1 Kings 4:24, where it is mentioned as the northeastern limit of Solomon's domain. It is juxtaposed with Gaza, which marks the southwestern limit, illustrating the vastness of the empire at its peak. This historical mention testifies to the extraordinary greatness of Solomon's reign, during which Israel extended from the Euphrates to the Egyptian borders.
H8607G.portee: This city reminds the Christian reader of the promise that God made to Solomon: unmatched wisdom and power (1 Kings 3:12-13). It symbolizes the pinnacle of prosperity and territorial expansion of Israel under a wise and obedient king. This contrast may also invite reflection on the fragility of human kingdoms and the importance of remaining obedient to God to maintain blessings.

sens: City in northern Israel, in the territory of the kingdom of Israel
Site of an extreme act of violence committed by King Menahem
H8607H.detail:
1. Thiphsach was a city located in the northern kingdom of Israel, probably a strategic point between Tirzah (the capital of Menahem at that time) and the northern regions. Its name means "passage" or "crossing," suggesting that it occupied an important position on trade or military routes.

2. This city is mentioned only once in the Bible, in 2 Kings 15:16, in a context of royal brutality: King Menahem attacked it because it refused to open its gates to him, and he committed atrocities against pregnant women there. This passage illustrates the political and military violence that characterized the last century of the northern kingdom.
H8607H.origine: The Hebrew name תִּפְסַח (Thiphsach) comes from a root meaning "to pass" or "to cross," evoking a ford or a crossing point. This geographical name likely reflects the function of the city: a crossroads or transit point. The name also appears in other ancient sources (Greek and Assyrian) in similar forms, confirming its strategic importance at the time.
H8607H.emploi: Thiphsach appears only once in the biblical text, in 2 Kings 15:16. It is mentioned during the reign of King Menahem, who ruled over Israel in the 8th century BC. The city had refused to submit to Menahem, who had seized the throne after assassinating Zachariah. In response, Menahem besieged the city, conquered it, and committed terrible violence against its population, particularly against pregnant women. This passage illustrates the political instability and cruelty that marked the decline of the northern kingdom.

sens: To hit a tambourine or percussion instrument to produce sounds
To strike oneself, as a sign of mourning or despair
H8608.detail:
1. The verb primarily denotes the action of playing the tambourine by striking it to make music. It is a joyful and festive gesture: in Psalm 68:26, young girls strike the tambourine amidst a procession of praise, alongside singers and musicians.
2. The verb can also mean to strike one's own chest or body as a sign of mourning, sorrow, or distress. In Nahum 2:8, the maidservants strike their chests like mourning doves, expressing their pain in the face of the destruction that befalls the city.
H8608.origine: The Hebrew verb תָּפַף (taphaf) comes from a root that imitates the sound of the strike: it is an onomatopoeic word that reproduces the sound "taf-taf" of the tambourine being struck. This root conveys the general idea of hitting or tapping on something. The word is related to other Hebrew verbs describing percussion actions.
H8608.emploi: The verb appears only twice in the Hebrew Bible. In Psalm 68:26, it describes the young girls playing the tambourine in a joyful religious celebration. In Nahum 2:8, it is used very differently: the maidservants are not making music; they are striking their chests in mourning before the fall of Nineveh. The same physical gesture — striking — changes completely in meaning depending on the context: joy or distress.
H8608.portee: This word reminds us that the same action — striking — can express either joy and praise or pain and mourning. For the Christian, it illustrates how our outward gestures take on meaning in the emotional and spiritual context we find ourselves in. It also invites us to recognize that true praise engages our whole being, body included.

sens: Join two pieces of fabric or material with thread and a needle
Assemble or create something by sewing
Dress or cover by sewing
Perform an act of sewing
H8609.detail:
1. To sew primarily means to join pieces of fabric together with thread: in Genesis 3:7, Adam and Eve, after eating the forbidden fruit and suddenly aware of their nakedness, sew together fig leaves to make themselves makeshift belts. This is the simplest image: putting thread in a needle and passing it through the fabric to hold two pieces together.
2. The verb extends to making or crafting objects by sewing: in Ezekiel 13:18, the prophetesses make cushions and veils by sewing them, which implies both the technical action and the finished result — the produced object.
3. To sew can also mean to dress or cover oneself with something by sewing it onto oneself: in Job 16:15, Job expresses his distress by saying, "I have sewn a sack on my skin," which evokes not only the act of sewing but also the state of the one wearing this sack, a symbol of mourning and penitence, like a garment attached to his body.
4. Figuratively, sewing appears in the context of cyclical human activities: in Ecclesiastes 3:7, there is "a time to sew" and "a time to tear," where the verb designates one of the regular and necessary actions of life, one of the tasks that each generation accomplishes.
H8609.origine: The Hebrew verb תָּפַר (tâphar) expresses the action of joining by sewing, literally "to bring in the thread." It belongs to the primitive root of sewing and weaving. The word has the simple and concrete meanings of any ancient manual activity: it describes a basic and universal technique, that of the needle and thread, known since ancient times for assembling clothing and household items.
H8609.emploi: This verb appears only four times in the Hebrew Bible, always to describe a concrete act of sewing or making. In Genesis 3:7, it is the inaugural act of sewing in the biblical narrative: the man and the woman, naked and ashamed, sew leaves to cover themselves — it is an act of human nature in the face of guilt, a mixture of self-awareness and an attempt to hide. In Job 16:15, sewing a sack on one's skin is an expression of extreme mourning: Job wears the traditional signs of misfortune. In Ecclesiastes 3:7, sewing is included in the list of periodic human activities, driven by the rhythm of time. In Ezekiel 13:18, the same verb describes the making of objects of magic or deception. The meaning remains concrete and practical, but it can carry a moral or theological significance depending on the context.
H8609.portee: The verb to sew reminds us that the body, shame, and covering are linked to the story of humanity from the beginning: in Genesis 3:7, it is the first act of the sinner aware of his nakedness. Furthermore, Ecclesiastes shows us that every human activity — including sewing — has its time, its hour, and that there is a given rhythm to life. It is an invitation to accept that not everything is done in the same way or at the same time, and that wisdom consists in discerning the right moment.

sens: Catch or hold something with the hand, take it in grip
Capture a person, stop or imprison them
Handle an object, hold and use it skillfully
Occupy or take possession of a place, territory
Be captured, arrested, caught in a trap (passive form)
H8610.detail:
1. To catch or hold something with the hand, to take it in grip: this is the basic action of closing the hand around an object to seize it. When Jubal "plays" the harp (Genesis 4:21), he seizes the instrument to produce sounds — the word describes this manual control and the first gesture of the musician.

2. To capture a person, to stop or imprison them: this is to seize someone to master them. When Joash "takes" King Agag alive (1 Samuel 15:8), he captures him in war; when the guards "seize" Jeremiah (Jeremiah 26:8), they arrest him by force.

3. To handle an object, to hold and use it skillfully: this is to seize a tool or a weapon to play with skill and authority. The verb describes the mastery one exercises over what one holds.

4. To occupy or take possession of a place, territory: this is to seize it militarily or permanently. When Sennacherib "takes" the cities of Judah (Isaiah 36:1), he conquers them; when one "occupies" the hilltops (Jeremiah 49:16), one establishes one's domain there.

5. To be captured, arrested, caught in a trap: this is the passive form of the verb, where one becomes the prey. When one is "caught" in a net (Ezekiel 17:20), one has become a slave to the trap.
H8610.origine: This Hebrew verb comes from a root that paints the motor image of the hand closing, the gesture of taking. The word family includes terms designating the grip, the hold. The verb appears in several forms: the simple form (Qal) describes the active action of seizing; the passive form (Niphal) describes the one who is seized; the intensive form (Piel) emphasizes the vigor or repetition of the gesture. It is a fundamental verb of action, of domination through taking.
H8610.emploi: This verb appears 60 times in the Old Testament, notably in accounts of war, capture, and control. It appears mainly in the historical books (Samuel, Kings), among the prophets (Jeremiah, Ezekiel), but also in the Psalms and Proverbs. The meaning varies slightly depending on the context: seizing a weapon or an instrument implies mastery and skill; capturing an enemy or a fugitive implies strength and authority; occupying a city implies military conquest or lasting control. The word can also describe the act of taking someone to accuse or punish them. The passive form emphasizes the vulnerability or helplessness of the one who is seized.
H8610.portee: This word reveals how the Bible views action: taking control is to exercise authority or responsibility. For the reader, it invites reflection on what one "seizes" — what goals, what values, what call from God. It also shows that no one escapes God's net, even if they flee: the final capture is inevitable for one who refuses His word. It is a word of spiritual realism, neither sweet nor violently accusatory.

sens: the act of spitting in someone's face
a mark of insult and humiliation
public rejection and shame
H8611.detail:
1. The word designates the act of spitting, a brutal gesture of insult and disgust towards a person. It is a direct affront, the physical expression of contempt (Job 17:6).
2. By extension, it means contempt itself, that is, the feeling of humiliation and rejection that results. The one treated this way becomes the target of collective shame.
3. It expresses public degradation and cursing: to be the object of contempt is to be rejected by one's community and stripped of all dignity.
H8611.origine: The word comes from a root that imitates the act of spitting (tpf in Hebrew). It is a concrete term that paints the visceral image of disgust: spitting as a symptom and symbol of total rejection. The word remains infrequent in biblical Hebrew and specifically designates this form of humiliation among the most brutal.
H8611.emploi: This word appears only once in the Hebrew Bible, in Job 17:6. Job laments having become a fable, a laughingstock, a target of insult and contempt for others. He speaks of his extreme degradation: his person is an object of contempt, which means he is treated as unworthy of respect. It is a cry of distress in the face of humiliation.
H8611.portee: Job's words remind us that contempt and insult are serious forms of injustice that God sees and cares about. The New Testament teaches us that Jesus himself suffered humiliation and contempt (Matthew 26:67), which allows Him to empathize with those who suffer rejection. It is a call to treat others with dignity and honor, even in suffering.

sens: place of burning in the south of Jerusalem
site of child sacrifices to false gods
symbol of God's anger and judgment
H8612.detail:
1. Topheth is a specific geographical location, situated in the valley of Ben-Hinnom (the valley of the sons of Hinnom) to the southeast of Jerusalem. The name literally means "place of fire" or "place of burning," as fires were lit there.
2. It became a site of religious abomination: unfaithful Israelites built high places there where they burned their own children as sacrifices to false gods, particularly to Molech (Jeremiah 7:31). King Josiah defiled this place to stop the worship (2 Kings 23:10).
3. Topheth becomes, in the mouths of the prophets, an image of divine judgment: God promises to transform this place of horror into a "valley of slaughter" where the inhabitants of Jerusalem will be buried without a place, symbolizing the complete ruin of the city (Jeremiah 7:32; 19:12). The place transitions from a cursed sanctuary to a mass grave.
H8612.origine: The Hebrew name means "place of fire" or "hearth of burning." It derives from the root related to fire and burning. Its association with the valley of Ben-Hinnom, where the fire of divine judgment once flowed according to tradition, makes it the quintessential symbol of damnation and destruction.
H8612.emploi: Topheth appears 8 times in the Old Testament, exclusively in the prophecies of Jeremiah (6 occurrences) and in the account of 2 Kings 23 (1 occurrence). All occurrences are situated between the 7th and 6th centuries B.C., during the time of King Josiah's religious reform and Jeremiah's preaching. The word first designates the actual high place of child sacrifices (Jeremiah 7:31), then becomes in Jeremiah a prophetic image of punishment: this infamous place will be transformed into a mass grave, and even its name will be replaced by "valley of slaughter" (Jeremiah 7:32; 19:6). Topheth thus embodies divine reversal: from a place of abomination to a place of ruin.
H8612.portee: Topheth reminds the believer that God abhors the sacrifice of the innocent and idolatry, no matter how deeply rooted they may be in a nation. For Jeremiah and his readers, this cursed place becomes a warning: the religious perversion of a people attracts God's inevitable judgment. The image of Topheth transformed into the valley of slaughter shows that divine power completely overturns the plans of rebels and makes abomination visible forever.

sens: place of idolatrous worship in the south of Jerusalem, in the valley of the son of Hinnom
H8613.detail: Topheth is a valley located at the southeastern end of the valley of the son of Hinnom, downstream from Jerusalem. It is here that the people of Israel, abandoning the true God, worshiped idols: offerings were burned there, including children in the fire of the god Molech. The prophet Isaiah refers to this place, comparing it to a burning pyre, a terrifying image of Gehenna where God judges evil (Isaiah 30:33). The very name, "place of fire," recalls the flames that consumed impious offerings there.
H8613.origine: The name Topheth comes from the word that means "hearth" or "place of fire." It is a symbol of destruction by fire, and in biblical prophetic preaching, this real place becomes the very image of the final condemnation of sin.
H8613.emploi: Topheth is mentioned in the Bible as the center of idolatrous worship in Israel, particularly under the kings who turned away from the Lord. The prophet Isaiah refers to it to threaten those who reject God: he compares Topheth to a pyre prepared to destroy God's enemies, announcing divine judgment.
H8613.portee: Topheth reminds the Christian reader of the fatal danger of idolatry and rejection of God. It is a warning: sin, taken to its extreme, leads to destruction. This place becomes in the Bible the figure of Gehenna, teaching that God does not leave unpunished those who despise Him and even sacrifice innocence for their false gods.

sens: Royal official in charge of administering a province or a matter of the kingdom
High-ranking judicial or administrative officer
H8614.detail:
1. The word designates a high official appointed by the king to govern a region or direct an important function in the empire. In Daniel 3:2, King Nebuchadnezzar summons the treasurers and judges among other magistrates of the provinces — these are men invested with authority to execute royal orders and oversee administration.
2. More broadly, it is a title given to any high-ranking officer or judge in the royal hierarchy. In Daniel 3:3, these magistrates assemble before the king's statue: they represent the established power and must obey the monarch's decrees.
H8614.origine: The Aramaic word תִּפְתָּיֵא (tiph-tay) likely comes from a root meaning "to judge" or "to cut." It describes one who exercises judicial or administrative authority. In imperial Aramaic, the language of Persian administration, this term was used to designate various categories of royal officials.
H8614.emploi: This word appears only twice in the Bible, in verses 2 and 3 of Daniel 3, both in the same passage. The context is unique: Nebuchadnezzar, king of Babylon, summons all the high officials of his empire — satraps, prefects, governors, judges, treasurers, and magistrates — to attend the consecration of a giant golden statue. These magistrates represent the machinery of royal power and the established authority that the three young Hebrews (Shadrach, Meshach, and Abednego) will challenge by refusing to bow down.
H8614.portee: This passage shows how earthly power structures, however impressive they may be — with all their magistrates and officials — must submit to God. The three young men choose to disobey the king's decree rather than renounce their faith. The word magistrate reminds us that human authority, even the highest, is never above obedience to God.

sens: Cord or woven tie, often brightly colored
Sign of recognition or covenant between people
H8615A.detail:
1. The word primarily designates a cord or string — a woven or knotted tie — that can be attached to a window or a wall. In the account of Joshua, Rahab ties a scarlet cord to her window in Joshua 2:18-21: it is a tangible, concrete object visible from afar.
2. This cord also becomes a sign of alliance and protection: the Jewish spies tell her, "tie this cord... to the window" as a mark of the covenant they make with her. This appears only in these two verses, but the object binds two enemy peoples in a mutual promise.
H8615A.origine: The Hebrew word tiqvah comes from a root that evokes the idea of binding or tying. It is a concrete word: a cord is what holds, what ties. The same root can elsewhere evoke waiting or hope (the underlying idea being what "holds" together). Here, we are at the heart of the material meaning: a cord, a woven thread that is visible and durable.
H8615A.emploi: This word appears only twice in the Old Testament, both in the account of Joshua 2 where Rahab, a prostitute from Jericho, helps the spies of Israel escape. The scarlet cord she ties to her window seals a covenant: her life and that of her family will be spared in exchange for her help. It is a humble yet powerful object of alliance that marks Rahab's passage to the side of God's people and foreshadows her place in the genealogy of Jesus (Matthew 1:5).
H8615A.portee: This crimson cord invites the reader to see how God honors even humble obedience and faith, even among outsiders. Rahab, a despised woman, finds salvation and honor through her trust in the God of Israel. This simple cord makes a covenant visible and reminds us that the concrete signs of the covenant carry weight in the eyes of God and men.

sens: Confident expectation of a good to come
Reason or motive to rely on something
What one desires to obtain or what may happen
State of one who does not despair
Foundation of trust in God
H8615B.detail:
1. Hope is primarily the expectation of a future good, a confidence directed towards tomorrow. Ruth, who has become a widow and is without resources, says to her daughters: "I am too old to marry again" — she no longer has hope for that future she might have had (Ruth 1:12). It is an expectation, a tension of the soul towards what is not yet.
2. Hope can also refer to the motive, the reason for hoping: it is what our trust rests upon. The psalmist cries out: "You are my hope, Lord!" (Psalms 71:5) — God Himself is the unshakeable foundation of his expectation.
3. Hope also names the thing hoped for, the object of desire: what one wishes to see realized. Jeremiah announces: "There is hope for your future... Your children will return to their own territory" (Jeremiah 31:17) — the return of the exiles is the promised hope.
4. It is the state opposite to despair. When hope fades, it is the death of the soul: "The hope of the wicked will perish" (Job 8:13), says the Wise — the one who forgets God loses all grip on the future.
5. In biblical language, hope is also a rope thrown to oneself in distress: Lamentations says "it is good to hope quietly" (Lamentations 3:29), for even without visible evidence, the soul can cling to God.
H8615B.origine: The Hebrew word tiqvah comes from a root meaning "to expect," "to look towards." It is related to the idea of tension, of a thread or cord — like a line stretched from now to tomorrow. The Hebrew word thus expresses not only a feeling but an active posture of the heart that stretches, that reaches towards what does not yet exist. It is never passivity; it is a movement of trust. The same root produces other words that speak of waiting and connection.
H8615B.emploi: The word hope appears 31 times in the Hebrew Bible, especially in the wisdom books (Job, Proverbs, Psalms) and among the prophets. In Job, it is tested by suffering: Job asks, "Where then is my hope?" when he is overwhelmed (Job 17:15), while his friends urge him not to lose hope (Job 4:6). In Proverbs, it is a moral strength: "For there is a future, and your hope will not be cut off" (Proverbs 23:18) — it supports the righteous and destroys the wicked. Among the prophets, particularly Jeremiah, hope becomes a political and spiritual promise (Jeremiah 29:11, 31:17): God Himself is the guarantor. It thus oscillates between personal feeling, theological foundation, and object of divine promise.
H8615B.portee: Biblical hope is not a vague optimism, but a virtue anchored in God. This word teaches the believer that looking to the future is a weapon against despair and a reasonable trust that God keeps His promises. It endures through trials: it is in suffering that hope proves true or false. It invites one to live in tension towards God, like a cord always stretched between today's trust and tomorrow's promises.

sens: Man from the time of the divided monarchy, father of Shallum
Character mentioned during the discovery of the Book of the Law under the reign of Josiah
H8616G.detail:
1. Tikvah is a man who lives at the time when the kingdom of Israel is divided into two: the kingdom of Judah and that of the North. He is the father of Shallum, who married the prophetess Huldah (2 Kings 22:14). His name means "hope" in Hebrew, a beautiful promise for his descendants.
2. He appears in the account of the religious reform under King Josiah of Judah, when the priest Hilkiah discovers the Book of the Law in the temple (2 Chronicles 34:22). The king's officials come to consult Huldah, the wife of his son Shallum, to know God's will regarding this crucial discovery.
H8616G.origine: The name Tikvah (תִּקְוָה) literally means "hope" or "expectation" in Hebrew. It comes from the root קוה (qavah), which expresses the idea of waiting with confidence, of placing one's hope in something or someone. Giving this name to a child was a way of expressing confidence in the future and in divine providence. It is a name rich in spiritual meaning, typical of Israelite spirituality.
H8616G.emploi: Tikvah is mentioned twice in the Bible, in two parallel passages that recount the same event with slight variations: 2 Kings 22:14 and 2 Chronicles 34:22. His historical importance mainly comes from his descendants: he is the grandfather of the prophetess Huldah, wife of the high priest or official Shallum. This man, although humble in the biblical narrative, is integrated into a pivotal moment in the history of Judah: the discovery of the Book of the Law under Josiah, which provokes a major religious reform. His existence and name remind us that even secondary characters in Scripture are part of God's great plans.

sens: Father of Jachzia during the time of Ezra
H8616H.detail: Thikva is a Jewish man from the time of exile and return, mentioned only once in the Bible. He is the father of Jachzia, who, along with a few others, opposed Ezra's measure regarding mixed marriages (Ezra 10:15).
H8616H.origine: The name Thikva means "hope" or "expectation" in Hebrew, from the root קוה (qavah) which means "to hope, to wait." It is a theophoric name that expresses trust in God's action, common among Jews of this period.
H8616H.emploi: Thikva appears only once in the Bible, in Ezra 10:15. He is mentioned as the father of Jachzia, one of the few men who opposed Ezra's policy ordering the Jews to put away their foreign wives. This brief mention situates him in the context of the return from exile and the reconstruction of the Jewish community.

sens: Ability to stand, to hold firm
Solidarity, stability in the face of adversity
Power of resistance against the enemy
H8617.detail:
1. The word primarily denotes the physical ability to stand, to hold one's ground. It is the image of the soldier who does not collapse.
2. By extension, it refers to moral stability and inner strength that allow one to stand firm in the face of trials. In Leviticus 26:37, it means that the people will not have the strength to maintain themselves, to subsist against their enemies: they will flee in disorder, unable to gather or resist.
3. The word thus expresses the power that allows one to persevere, to not bend under pressure. It is the opposite of collapse and flight.
H8617.origine: The word comes from the root קום (qoum), which means "to rise," "to stand up." It is a fundamental verb in Hebrew, expressing the action of taking a stand, of resisting, of persevering. The noun תְּקוּמָה adds the idea of permanence and capacity: it is not only the action of rising, but the strength to be and to remain standing.
H8617.emploi: This word appears only once in the Hebrew Bible, in Leviticus 26:37. It is a word of threat addressed by God to the people of Israel: if the people do not follow Him, God will ensure that they will not subsist before their enemies. The image is that of a military debacle: the Israelites will topple over one another, unable to form a solid resistance. The word thus expresses complete collapse, the loss of all capacity to stand together and persevere.
H8617.portee: This word reminds us of a profound spiritual truth: our stability and victory do not come from ourselves, but from our relationship with God. Only faithfulness to the covenant with the Lord gives us the strength to subsist in the face of trials and enemies. It is an invitation to place our trust in God rather than in our own strength.

sens: To stand face to face with someone in hostility
To take a stand against, to oppose firmly
H8618.detail:
1. To rise up against means to stand up, to lift oneself in front of someone while showing hostility or rebellion. It is the image of someone who rises to confront an opponent. In Psalm 139:21, the psalmist expresses his disgust towards those who rise up against God: those who stand as declared enemies against Him.
2. More broadly, it means to take a stand against someone, to oppose with declared hostility. The verb expresses not only a physical or verbal act but also an attitude of deliberate and overt rebellion.
H8618.origine: The Hebrew word תְּקוֹמֵם comes from the root קוּם (qoum), which means "to rise, to stand up" — the fundamental image of vertical movement, of lifting up. The reflexive form (hithpol) adds the idea of raising oneself, of actively taking a stand. This root is very common in biblical Hebrew and creates several words expressing the idea of resurrection, establishment, or uprising. Here, it produces the image of standing against someone, an active and declared opposition.
H8618.emploi: This verb appears only once in the Hebrew Bible, in Psalm 139:21. In this context, it describes the attitude of God's enemies, those who rise up against Him and hate Him. The psalmist, in praise of God who knows him perfectly, expresses his union with divine justice: he hates those who hate God and shows disgust towards those who rise up against Him. This unique occurrence shows the use of the verb in a context of spiritual and moral conflict.
H8618.portee: This word reminds us that opposition to God is never neutral or passive: it is an active revolt, a declared uprising. For the Christian, this invites recognition of the real stakes of spiritual struggle and reflection on the seriousness of the position one takes before God. It is also an invitation to align the heart with divine justice.

sens: Metal wind instrument to produce loud sounds
Signal of alert or call to battle or during a disaster
Solemn announcement, public proclamation
H8619.detail:
1. The trumpet is a metal wind instrument that produces powerful and piercing sounds. It is a concrete object, a utensil of war or ceremony. In Ezekiel 7:14, the trumpet is sounded to gather warriors for battle: it is an audible signal from very far away.
2. The sound of the trumpet serves to alert, to call people to action — notably to take up arms or to flee danger. In Ezekiel, despite the trumpet's call, no one responds to the call to battle, which shows the terror and defeat that overwhelm the city.
3. By extension, the trumpet becomes the symbol of a grave announcement, a solemn public message. It evokes the idea of a proclamation that imposes itself on all, which cannot be ignored.
H8619.origine: The Hebrew word תָּקוֹעַ comes from a root that means "to strike, to give a blow." The trumpet is the instrument that is "struck" or "blown" to produce this sound. This word specifically designates this wind instrument, distinct from other musical or signaling instruments.
H8619.emploi: This word appears only once in the Hebrew Bible, in Ezekiel 7:14, in a vision of judgment on Jerusalem. The context is one of military catastrophe: God announces that judgment is coming, and although the trumpet is sounded to mobilize the warriors, no one rises to battle. The trumpet symbolizes here the call to resistance that goes unanswered, thus marking total abandonment and defeat.
H8619.portee: This word reminds us that God can cry out alert and call, but it is up to the people to respond. When no one answers God's call, it is a sign of deep disobedience and its terrible consequences. For the believer, the trumpet is an image of the divine cry that demands an immediate response.

sens: City of the kingdom of Judah, in the mountainous region near Hebron
Birthplace of the prophet Amos
H8620.detail:
1. Tekoa is a city built in Judea in the hills, not far from Hebron. It was first founded by Ashhur, son of Hezron, and then rebuilt by King Rehoboam of Judah as a fortified place (2 Chronicles 11:6). It served as a strategic point: in case of invasion from the north, an alert could be sounded there to warn Jerusalem (Jeremiah 6:1).
2. Tekoa is famous for being the birthplace and origin of the prophet Amos. It is from this small provincial town that this farmer prophet arose, sent by God to announce His message of justice to the kingdoms of Israel and Judah (Amos 1:1).
H8620.origine: The name literally means "a cutting off" or "a fortification" — the image of a protected place, surrounded by palisades. This etymology well reflects the military role of this city in the defenses of the kingdom of Judah.
H8620.emploi: Tekoa is mentioned seven times in the Bible, almost always in the context of the geography or political history of Judah. Besides its founding and reconstruction by the kings of Judah, it appears as a point of alert in case of invasion (Jeremiah 6:1). It enters the royal annals as the place where King Jehoshaphat gathered the inhabitants for a declaration of trust in God (2 Chronicles 20:20). Its importance exceeds its size: it is the cradle of the prophet Amos, who made it the starting point of his prophetic ministry against injustice.
H8620.portee: Tekoa reminds us that God chooses His messengers from the most humble and unexpected places. Amos, coming from this small town, brings the divine word with the same authority as any court prophet. This encourages the believer: spiritual greatness and importance do not come from social position or worldly prestige, but from God's calling.

sens: City of Judea, located south of Jerusalem
Inhabitant of Tekoa
H8621.detail:
1. Tekoa is a city of Judea located south of Jerusalem, in an arid region. It is from there that the wise woman intervened with King David to reconcile Amnon and Absalom (2 Samuel 14:4).
2. A Tekoite is an inhabitant of Tekoa. Ira, son of Ikkesh, from Tekoa, was one of David's most renowned warriors and commanded a military division (1 Chronicles 27:9). The Tekoites also participated in the reconstruction of the wall of Jerusalem after the exile (Nehemiah 3:5).
H8621.origine: The name Tekoa comes from a Hebrew root that evokes the sound of the trumpet (tekoa literally means "sound of the trumpet"). It is a common place name in biblical geography, designating a well-established city in the mountains of Judah.
H8621.emploi: Tekoa appears 7 times in the Hebrew Bible. It is primarily a city from which several important figures come: the wise woman before David, the warrior Ira, and the Tekoites who contribute to the reconstruction of the wall under Nehemiah. The term "Tekoite" is used as a demographic adjective to designate one who comes from Tekoa.
H8621.portee: Tekoa reminds us that God uses ordinary people from remote places — a woman without official power, warriors, workers — to accomplish His purposes. It is an invitation to recognize that wisdom and service to God are not reserved for large cities or elites.

sens: Passage d'une période de temps qui revient régulièrement, particulièrement d'une année
Accomplissement ou parcours complet d'une trajectoire ou d'un chemin
Terme qui désigne le mouvement circulaire ou la boucle qui ramène au point de départ
H8622.detail:
1. The word expresses the idea of a period that "turns" and returns: a year that is completed from beginning to end ("when the year was completed" in 2 Chronicles 24:23), or the natural course of time that flows regularly ("in the course of the year" in 1 Samuel 1:20). It is like a cycle that closes.
2. It also describes the complete path of a trajectory: the sun "completes its course" (Psalms 19:7), meaning it travels its path from one end to the other of the sky. The image is that of a road or an orbit that comes to an end.
3. The word can simply evoke the notion of "end" ("at the end of the year" in Exodus 34:22), the moment when a period concludes and closes the loop it has described.
H8622.origine: The word comes from a Hebrew root that means "to turn" or "to turn oneself." It evokes circular movement, return: something that turns to form a closed loop. That is why it applies to cycles that return (the years) and to paths that are completed.
H8622.emploi: This word appears only four times in the Hebrew Bible. It is primarily used to designate the completion or end of a year, from the beginning to the end of its revolution (Exodus 34:22, 1 Samuel 1:20, 2 Chronicles 24:23). Only once, in Psalms 19:7, does it describe the course of the sun in the sky, its complete path from one extremity to the other. The meaning remains constant: a period or a path that concludes after following its natural course.
H8622.portee: This word invites us to recognize that time flows in regular cycles according to God's plan, and that each season, each year has its fulfillment. It also reminds us that creatures, like the sun, faithfully complete their course: nothing escapes divine order, and everything follows its path to the end.

sens: Qui a une grande force physique ou morale
Qui est puissant, capable de résister ou de dominer
H8623.detail:
1. The word describes someone who possesses remarkable strength, a power that allows them to act effectively or impose their will. In Ecclesiastes 6:10, the weak man cannot "contend with one stronger than himself" — meaning he cannot dispute or compete with one who surpasses him in power. It is the brute or moral strength of a person capable of prevailing.
2. Figuratively, the term can evoke solidity, the ability to stand firm in the face of adversity or to dominate a situation. It is the unwavering power of one who has the means to assert their will.
H8623.origine: This Aramaic word belongs to the language spoken in Northern Arabia and Mesopotamia. It is related to the Hebrew תָּקַף (taqaph), which means "to be strong" or "to be powerful." The root evokes the idea of strength, solidity, and the ability to resist or dominate. The Aramaic taqquiph is the adjective derived from this root, formed to express the quality of one who is strong.
H8623.emploi: The word appears only once in the Bible, in Ecclesiastes 6:10, a passage partly written in Aramaic. The Ecclesiastes uses it to express a universal truth: the weak man cannot compete or dispute with one who is stronger than himself. It is an observation of the human condition in the face of forces that surpass us — whether they are natural, social, or even divine. The context emphasizes the relative powerlessness of the ordinary man.
H8623.portee: This word reminds the Christian reader that in the face of forces that surpass us — evil, injustice, our own limitations — we can only rely on an external power. For the believer, it is an opportunity to acknowledge their weakness and to turn to God, who is infinitely stronger. Humility before what surpasses us is thus a path to wisdom.

sens: Qui possède une grande force physique ou une grande puissance
Qui est imposant, impressionnant par sa solidité ou sa capacité à dominer
Qui exerce une autorité, une domination remarquable
H8624.detail:
1. The word describes what is strong, robust, capable of exercising formidable force. In Daniel 2:40, the fourth kingdom is compared to iron: "strong as iron; just as iron breaks and crushes everything, it will break and crush everything" — it is the image of a destructive and irresistible power.
2. It also qualifies what is solid and imposing in its structure or domination. In Daniel 2:42, the same kingdom is "partly strong and partly fragile," mixing areas of absolute solidity with others that are more fragile, like a disparate empire.
3. The word applies to remarkable authority or majesty. In Daniel 4:3, the "mighty wonders" of the Most High highlight the extent of His acts; in Ezra 4:20, the "mighty kings" of Jerusalem are those who master the lands and receive tribute — a political and administrative power.
H8624.origine: This Aramaic word (the language spoken in Babylon) is the Aramaic form of the Hebrew תַּקִּיף (taqîph). It expresses the idea of brute strength, of solidity that does not yield. The root evokes something tight, compact, robust — the image of what holds firm and crushes the obstacle.
H8624.emploi: This Aramaic word appears five times, all in the Aramaic passages of Daniel and Ezra (chapters where the Aramaic speakers are present). It primarily qualifies kingdoms or political powers: the fourth kingdom (Daniel 2:40, 2:42, 7:7) is described as extraordinarily strong, with iron teeth, capable of crushing everything around it. It also describes the strength of the ancient kings of Jerusalem (Ezra 4:20) and the power of divine wonders (Daniel 4:3). In each case, it emphasizes an overwhelming superiority, an unmatched domination.
H8624.portee: This word reminds us that in history, there are formidable powers — human or divine — that shape empires and peoples. For the Christian reader, it invites us to recognize that only divine power is truly eternal and unshakeable, while all earthly kingdoms, no matter how strong, are fragile and destined to pass away.

sens: Déterminer ou vérifier le poids de quelque chose en le mettant sur une balance
Être mis en balance, être évalué
Être reconnu comme insuffisant ou léger
H8625A.detail:
1. The word describes the action of putting something on a scale to know its weight: it is an act of measurement and precise verification. In Daniel 5:27, King Belshazzar is "weighed in the balance," as if he were a commodity being evaluated.
2. More broadly, being "weighed" means being measured, judged, put to the test: God weighs the hearts and actions of men, subjecting them to a rigorous examination.
3. The result can be negative: being found "light" (as in the passage from Daniel) means being judged insufficient, inadequate, unworthy — the weight does not meet the standard. It is a discreet but terrible condemnation: one is judged and does not pass the test.
H8625A.origine: The word comes from a root that means "to be light" or "to be light in weight." In Hebrew, "to weigh" and "to be light" are closely related: what is weighed can be found light, hence the idea of judgment or insufficiency. The form used here (pi'el) intensifies the action: one does not just weigh, one weighs truly, actively, to verify.
H8625A.emploi: The word appears only once in the Bible in this precise form, at the decisive moment of Belshazzar's feast (Daniel 5:27). It is a scene of divine judgment: while the king profanes by drinking from the sacred vessels of the temple of Jerusalem, an invisible hand writes on the wall "Mene, Mene, Tekel, Upharsin" — that is, "Numbered, Numbered, Weighed, Divided." The prophet Daniel explains that "Tekel" means "You have been weighed in the balance, and you have been found wanting": the king has been judged, measured against God's justice, and he has failed. His reign is over.
H8625A.portee: For the Christian reader, this word reminds us that God scrutinizes the hearts and actions of each person: we are all measured, weighed. It is an invitation to self-examination and spiritual seriousness. But also an assurance: this divine judgment is just and inevitable. Our value does not rest on our appearances or our riches, but on our faithfulness to God.

sens: Determine the weight of something on a scale
Evaluate, judge the value or merit of someone
Find someone insufficient, declare them light
H8625B.detail:
1. To weigh primarily means to place something on a scale to know its exact weight. It is the physical action of measuring: one places the object on one side and adds weights on the other until balance is achieved. In Daniel 5:25, the mysterious inscription displayed on the wall during King Belshazzar's feast bears this word: "Numbered, numbered, weighed."
2. To weigh can also mean to examine someone, evaluate their conduct, heart, or moral value — much like one weighs an object to know its true substance. It is a judgment.
3. When the scale tips too lightly on one side, it is said that that side has been "weighed" and found light: insufficient, deficient. In Daniel 5:27, the continuation of the vision explains: "You have been weighed in the balance, and found wanting" — King Belshazzar is judged unworthy, his actions do not carry the weight they should have.
H8625B.origine: The Hebrew word תְּקֵל (teqel) comes from a root that means to weigh, balance. In Aramaic (the language of the passage in Daniel), this root expresses the physical action of weighing on a scale. The word is related to the term שׁקֶל (sheqel), the well-known currency and unit of weight in Israel: the sheqel was originally a stone used for weighing before becoming a standard weight metal coin.
H8625B.emploi: The word appears only twice in the Bible, both in Daniel 5, in the famous passage of the mysterious writing on the wall of the royal palace. King Belshazzar hosts a great idolatrous feast when a supernatural hand writes on the wall: "Mene, mene, teqel, upharsin" — the Aramaic version. These three words describe a divine judgment pronounced on the king. While "mene" means numbered and "upharsin" means divided, "teqel" (weighed) specifically expresses the idea of judgment: God weighs the king in the moral balance, and finds him wanting. The two verses give the same formula: in verse 25, the inscription is reported; in verse 27, the prophet Daniel's response explains what this means for the king.
H8625B.portee: This word reminds us that God judges hearts and actions like a judge who weighs everything scrupulously. Nothing escapes His examination. To be "weighed" in the divine balance is a sobering image: it means that our lives are evaluated according to the true weight of our deeds and intentions, not on appearances. For the believer, it is a call to live with integrity, aware that God knows the true weight of our choices.

sens: Make straight, undo a curve
Arrange, put in order
Establish, confirm, make stable
H8626.detail:
1. To make straight, undo a curve: the word expresses the action of transforming what is bent or twisted into something straight. It is a concrete physical movement. Ecclesiastes uses it twice to say that what is bent by God cannot be straightened by man: "What is crooked cannot be made straight" (Ecclesiastes 1:15), and "who can make straight what He has made crooked?" (Ecclesiastes 7:13).
2. To arrange, put in order: the word takes on a broader meaning and refers to the organization, the regular arrangement of several things. Ecclesiastes says he has "set in order a great number of sayings" (Ecclesiastes 12:11), meaning he has classified them, organized them coherently.
3. To establish, confirm, make stable: particularly in Aramaic, the verb acquires the meaning of confirming or establishing something durably. It is the idea that something becomes firm and assured.
H8626.origine: The verb comes from a Hebrew root that fundamentally evokes the idea of straightness and uprightness. The primary image is that of a straight line, of rectification. The root is found in other Hebrew words related to rule, order, and arrangement. In Aramaic, the same verb (תְּקַן) has strengthened its meaning towards "confirm" or "establish," showing how vocabulary evolves between biblical Hebrew and Aramaic.
H8626.emploi: The verb appears only three times in the Hebrew Bible, all in Ecclesiastes. Twice, it expresses the idea that one cannot straighten what God has bent: it is an affirmation of human incapacity to modify divine order. A third time, it describes the activity of the wise man who organizes his teachings. The context of Ecclesiastes makes it a word of reflection: the author uses it to express the limits of human wisdom in the face of God's works, and also the order that the wise brings to the words.
H8626.portee: This word invites the reader to recognize the limits of their power: there are things that only God can rectify or transform deeply. For those who teach or convey faith, it also reminds the importance of bringing order and clarity to words, as Ecclesiastes did with his sayings.

sens: Put in order, organize
Make stable, consolidate
Affirm with certainty, confirm
Restore after an interruption
H8627.detail:
1. This word primarily speaks of putting things in good order, arranging them so that they function correctly — the idea of something well organized and structured.
2. It also means to make something stable and durable, to consolidate it so that it holds and persists — like laying a solid foundation so that a building does not wobble.
3. It expresses the action of confirming, affirming something strongly so that no one contests it — giving it certainty.
4. It can finally refer to the act of restoring, of reestablishing after a break: in Daniel 4:36, after Nebuchadnezzar loses his reason and his kingship, his reason is restored to him, and his royal authority is returned and affirmed.
H8627.origine: This Hebrew verb comes from a root that first evokes the idea of standing up, of raising. The basic image is that of something being straightened, held firm so that it does not collapse. The form used here (hophal) is a passive form that suggests an external action that strengthens something — it is not the thing itself that stabilizes, but someone or something that stabilizes it.
H8627.emploi: This verb appears only once in the Bible, in Daniel 4:36. It is a key text: King Nebuchadnezzar recounts how, after being struck with madness for seven years, his reason was restored to him and his royal dignity affirmed again. The context is one of miraculous and divine restoration — it is God who restores what had been destroyed. The word expresses not only the return to the previous state but also the confirmation, the new strengthening of that kingship.
H8627.portee: This term reminds the believer that only God can truly establish, strengthen, and restore what is fragile or broken. The implicit promise is that the Lord can restore a life, an authority, a dignity that sin or circumstances have destroyed — an encouragement for those who feel fallen or lost.

sens: Produce a sound with a trumpet or wind instrument
Strike, hit, give a blow
Drive in, plant firmly in the ground
Establish a covenant or commitment through a solemn gesture
H8628.detail:
1. Sounding the trumpet: this means making a wind instrument resonate to alert, assemble the people, or mark an important event. In Joshua 6:8, the priests "sound" loud trumpets during the march around Jericho. In Psalms 81:4, the trumpet is sounded at festivals to call the assembly.
2. Strike or hit: to deliver a sharp and vigorous blow with force. In Judges 4:21, Jael "drives" a tent peg through Sisera's head by striking it with a hammer. This is a violent and decisive act.
3. Drive in, set up: to plant something firmly in the ground, like a tent. In Genesis 31:25, Jacob "sets up" his tent on the mountain by planting it firmly. The image is one of a quick and sure action.
4. Solemnly commit: to make a solemn commitment, often by giving one’s word or striking the hand of a third party to seal an agreement. In Proverbs 6:1, "striking the hand" of a third party means to act as a guarantor for him, creating a legal obligation.
H8628.origine: The verb תָּקַע (taqua) comes from a root that expresses the idea of striking, delivering a sharp and energetic blow. This root evokes both the physical action of the blow and the resulting sound effect. That is why the word means both "to sound the trumpet" (to make a blow that produces a sound) and "to drive in" (to deliver a blow that embeds something in the ground). The same root appears in other Hebrew words related to the idea of striking or hitting.
H8628.emploi: The verb תָּקַע appears about 63 times in the Old Testament, mainly in the historical books (Samuel, Kings, Chronicles) and the prophets. Its most common meaning is "to sound the trumpet": it is a military, liturgical, or civil signal to assemble the people, give an alert, or mark a ceremony. Thus, in Judges 7:19-22, Gideon and his men sound the trumpet to surprise the enemy army. In 1 Kings 1:34 and 1:39, the trumpet is sounded to proclaim a new king. In the Psalms and Jeremiah, sounding the trumpet announces God's judgment or calls to prayer. The verb is also used for "driving in" or "setting up": in Genesis 31:25, setting up a tent; in Isaiah 22:23, driving in a nail. In Proverbs, "sounding" (or "striking") takes on the meaning of "committing one's word": striking the hand of a guarantor means making a solemn commitment.
H8628.portee: This word reminds us of how central sound and signal are in the life of Israel. The trumpet is not just a simple instrument: it is the voice of God calling, assembling, warning. It unites the people around a common action and obedience to God. For the believer today, sounding the trumpet evokes the urgency of proclaiming the Gospel, calling to repentance, and gathering the church around the Word of God. It is also a call to act with firmness and commitment: like a nail being driven in, like a covenant sealed by a decisive gesture.

sens: The sound produced by a trumpet or wind instrument
A call or sound signal that gathers or warns
A resounding sound that announces an important event
H8629.detail:
1. The word primarily designates the direct sound, the audible vibration that comes from a trumpet or horn. It is the characteristic, clear, and powerful noise produced by the instrument when played. In Psalms 150:3, God is celebrated by playing the trumpet: the term evokes this vibrant and resonant sound.
2. Beyond the simple noise, the sound of the trumpet is a call: it gathers people, warns them, mobilizes them. In ancient Jewish life, this sound announced serious or solemn events, moments when the entire people had to rise and listen.
3. The sound of the trumpet is also a signal of something great, divine, solemn: when God intervenes or when He is worshiped, the trumpet sounds. It is a sound that impresses and marks the minds.
H8629.origine: The Hebrew word comes from a root that means "to drive in," "to pierce," "to give a blow." The trumpet itself is called in Hebrew *shophar* or *chatsotsra*: it is an instrument that is blown to produce this powerful sound. The verb *taqua* means "to sound the trumpet" or "to emit a resounding sound." The word téqa is a nominal form of it: it retains the idea of the blow, the sound that strikes the ear and penetrates deeply.
H8629.emploi: The word appears only once in the Bible, in Psalms 150:3, where it is part of a hymn of praise to God. The context is musical and liturgical: an invitation to praise the Lord with various instruments, including the trumpet. It is a rare, specialized word, reserved for the precise notation of the sound of this instrument in religious celebration.
H8629.portee: For the reader, this word reminds us that praising God involves the body, the voice, and instruments. The sound of the trumpet is not silent or discreet: it is a joyful, resounding proclamation that requires courage and conviction. Praising God "with the sound of the trumpet" means doing so without shame, in a striking and public manner.

sens: Attack with force and vigor
Invade, overwhelm someone
Dominate, prevail over
H8630.detail:
1. Assail means to attack someone with force and intensity, like an enemy pouncing on its prey. It is a brutal and direct action: "Distress and anguish "assail" him like a king ready to fight" (Job 15:24).

2. The word can also describe a power that invades and overwhelms, pressing from all sides relentlessly. God Himself can assail man, striking him continually: "You are continually "assailed," and he goes away" (Job 14:20), an image of water eroding stone.

3. Finally, assail means to dominate, to prevail over someone or something. It carries the sense of strength and superiority: "If someone is stronger than one, the two can resist him" (Ecclesiastes 4:12), where being stronger means prevailing.
H8630.origine: The Hebrew verb תָּקֵף (taqaph) comes from a root that expresses strength, vigor, and intensity. The image is that of a power actively exerting itself, striking or imposing itself. This root also appears in nominal forms meaning "strength" or "vigor." The Hebrew word is based on the idea of pressing, applying strong pressure.
H8630.emploi: The verb תָּקֵף appears only three times in the Hebrew Bible, all occurrences found in the wisdom books (Job and Ecclesiastes). In the Book of Job, the word describes the action of God assailing man or that of calamitous forces overwhelming (distress, anguish). In Ecclesiastes, it expresses the notion of strength or numerical superiority. The context is always one of struggle, pressure, or the domination of one power over another. The meaning remains constant: a force that imposes itself.
H8630.portee: This word invites the reader to recognize the intensity of the trials that God may allow, without denying His justice or authority. It also speaks to the importance of unity and mutual support: alone, one is fragile; together, one becomes strong. For the believer, it is an invitation not to rely on one's own strength, but to seek the support of God and the community.

sens: To become powerful, robust, solid in physical structure
To become strong, vigorous, in a person or their authority
To harden, become insensitive or arrogant in heart and spirit
To make strong, strengthen, give solidity
To make strict, severe, rigorous in a law or order
H8631.detail:
1. The word primarily evokes the physical strength of something: the tree in the dream of the Babylonian king "had become great and strong," capable of standing tall and being seen from afar (Daniel 4:11).
2. It also applies to the power of a person: the king who became "great and strong" whose "greatness was increased" (Daniel 4:22), referring to his growing political authority.
3. Figuratively, it designates the hardening of the heart: the heart of the king rises and "hardens to arrogance," meaning it becomes inflexible, closed to reason, swollen with pride (Daniel 5:20).
4. The verb can also mean "to make strong" or "to strengthen": to give something the necessary solidity or resistance.
5. Applied to a law or decree, it means "to make severe or rigorous": the royal decree is issued "with a severe prohibition," that is, with rigor and threat of punishment (Daniel 6:7).
H8631.origine: The Aramaic word תְּקֵף (teqeph) comes from a root that expresses the idea of solidity and resistance. The same root exists in Hebrew and other Semitic languages. The basic image is that of a structure or a person becoming dense, compact, unshakeable. The word appears in several forms: a simple form "to grow strong" and an intensive form "to make strong" or "to strengthen," allowing the verb to describe both a change of state and an action by an external agent.
H8631.emploi: This Aramaic verb appears five times in the book of Daniel (Aramaic), which occupies a central place in the text. It first describes the physical and symbolic growth of the tree in the king's dream (Daniel 4:11 and 4:20), then applies to the king himself who has become powerful (Daniel 4:22). The word changes register in Daniel 5:20, where it designates the spiritual hardening of the king, his refusal to acknowledge God despite warnings. Finally, in Daniel 6:7, it qualifies the royal decree as a strict and relentless law. The context of the five uses shows how power and strength, when not accompanied by wisdom and humility before God, lead to pride, downfall, and hardness of heart.
H8631.portee: This word invites the reader to reflect on the true nature of strength. The Bible shows here that becoming "strong" without God—in political power or in refusal to listen—is in reality to lose oneself: the hardening of the heart precedes ruin. True strength is that which acknowledges God and remains humble, as Jesus will remind: "Whoever wants to be great among you must be your servant" (Matthew 20:26).

sens: power, physical or moral vigor
capacity to accomplish a great work
H8632A.detail:
1. Strength refers to power, vigor—the capacity to produce an effect, to accomplish. It is the word for raw power, the vigor that acts and realizes.
2. It particularly applies to human strength that builds, that creates great works: in Daniel 4:30, the king of Babylon attributes the construction of the magnificent city to his own strength, showing the pride of one who forgets that all power comes from God.
H8632A.origine: The Aramaic word תְּקָף (force) derives from the verb תְּקַף which means "to be strong, to be powerful." It is a Semitic term expressing the capacity to act with vigor. The root evokes the idea of firmness and solidity—one that holds firm, that does not yield.
H8632A.emploi: This word appears only once in the Bible, in Aramaic, in the speech of King Nebuchadnezzar in Daniel 4:30. There it designates the king's personal strength, that by which he claims to have built Babylon. The context is one of human pride: the king attributes to his own strength and magnificence a work that he should attribute to God. That is why God punishes him immediately afterward for this vanity.
H8632A.portee: This word highlights the spiritual danger of human pride: attributing to one's own strength what comes from God. For the Christian reader, it reminds that all power, all true accomplishment comes from God, and that claiming strength without acknowledging the divine source is the path to downfall.

sens: Physical or military power
Authority, command power
Capacity to accomplish or dominate
H8632B.detail:
1. The word first designates a concrete power, that which acts and imposes itself—the brute force of an army, the capacity to fight and conquer. In Daniel 2:37, God grants King Nebuchadnezzar the empire, the power, and the strength: it is the vigor that allows him to reign over the peoples.

2. It also signifies the authority and power that a sovereign exercises—not only physical capacity but the legitimacy and domination recognized by those who obey him. It is strength as an established reign.

3. More broadly, it is the capacity to impose one's will, to act effectively, and to hold to what one undertakes—a strength that is not only military but also political and administrative.
H8632B.origine: This Aramaic word is related to the Hebrew תֹּקֶף (toqeph), which also means "power" or "authority." The root evokes the idea of striking, pushing, forcing—something that imposes itself with vigor. The word belongs to the vocabulary of royal and divine power.
H8632B.emploi: The word appears only once in the Bible, in Daniel 2:37, where Nebuchadnezzar is recognized as king to whom God has given the empire, power, strength, and glory. This royal and divine context shows that strength here is a divine gift, an attribute of the sovereign power that God grants to the monarch. It is an organized strength, recognized, embodied in the established reign.
H8632B.portee: This word reminds the reader that all true authority—every true power—comes from God and remains under His control. Human strength, even that of a great empire, is but a delegated gift from the Lord of heaven.
