1. Concrete help: this is the assistance provided at the moment of danger. Joab says to Abishai: "If the Syrians are stronger than I, you will come to my aid" (1 Chronicles 19:12) — this is a military intervention to pull someone out of a predicament.
2. Victory: the word can also refer to success achieved in battle, which delivers from danger. This is why we speak of "salvation" where the Segond also translates as "victory."
3. Deliverance: this means being pulled from a mortal peril or from servitude. Jeremiah awaits deliverance from the Lord (Jeremiah 3:23), that is, to be brought out of distress.
4. Spiritual forgiveness: "The salvation of the righteous comes from the Lord" (Psalms 37:39) — this is no longer just being saved from a visible enemy, but being restored in relationship with God. This is the heart of the biblical message.
5. Inner rejoicing: "Those who love your salvation say continually: Exalted be the Lord!" (Psalms 40:17) — this is a state of peace and gratitude, the joy of being loved and protected by God.
H8668G.origine: The Hebrew word comes from a root that means "to be wide, spacious" — the primary image is that of an open passage, a deliverance that expands. From the same family comes "Joshua" (Yeshua in Hebrew), which literally means "the Lord saves." The corresponding Greek word in the Septuagint, "soteria" (σωτηρία), carries the same dual meaning: concrete salvation (military, physical) and spiritual salvation (restoration with God).
H8668G.emploi: The word occurs 21 times in the Hebrew Bible, especially in the Psalms and the prophets. In the early books (1 Samuel), it refers to military help, tangible assistance. In the Psalms (37, 40, 71, 119), it gradually takes on the hue of spiritual salvation: this is what the psalmist asks of God, in which he hopes, that which brings him joy. In Isaiah (45, 46), salvation becomes God's great project for His people: He promises eternal salvation, a definitive restoration. The word shifts from the military and human domain to the spiritual and divine domain, without ever losing the sense of a true and concrete deliverance.
H8668G.portee: This word invites the Christian to recognize that salvation is not limited to temporary material assistance, but is primarily the work of God who pulls us from sin and death. It shows that seeking salvation in God means placing one's hope not in human forces ("Do not put your trust in princes," Psalms 146:3) but in the one who can truly save the soul. It is also a reason for deep and constant rejoicing when one has discovered this salvation in God.

sens: Victory over an enemy
Liberation from danger or oppression
Help provided by God
Spiritual salvation granted by God
H8668H.detail:
1. The word primarily denotes a military victory, a victory achieved through combat: when Samson prays after defeating a thousand Philistines, he speaks of "this great deliverance" he has accomplished (Judges 15:18). It is a concrete victory over the enemy.

2. But it also describes a broader liberation, a deliverance from all oppression: when the Lord "works a deliverance" through his servants, he saves his people from peril (2 Samuel 23:10). The word evokes relief, the end of a threat.

3. More profoundly, it is God alone who can truly effect deliverance: it always comes from his hand, although it may pass through men. Naaman is an example: "it was by him that the Lord had delivered the Syrians" (2 Kings 5:1) — the man is the instrument, but God is the author.

4. Finally, the word can refer to spiritual salvation, the deliverance of the soul: it is an invisible victory that God wins on behalf of those who trust him, a liberation from sin and death.
H8668H.origine: The word comes from a Hebrew root that means "to be wide, spacious": deliverance is having space to breathe, escaping the narrowness of danger. It expresses the idea of a liberation that opens a new future. The word is close to other Hebrew terms for salvation and victory, all carrying this image of moving from a closed situation to a free one.
H8668H.emploi: This word appears 11 times in the Old Testament, mainly in historical and poetic narratives: in Judges, Kings, Chronicles, and in the Psalms and Proverbs. The usages always show a concrete deliverance: military victories achieved with God's help (Samson, Eleazar, Shammah), protection of peoples, help from the Lord. The word never denotes a human victory alone: it always emphasizes God's action. Gradually, from narrative to prayer, it takes on a more spiritual significance, becoming a sign that God watches over those who trust him.
H8668H.portee: This word speaks to the heart of the Christian by reminding that God is active and faithful: he intervenes to deliver his people from peril and sin. Each mention of deliverance strengthens trust in God's power and goodness. It invites the reader to recognize that their own liberation — in the face of temptations, anxieties, and death — comes from God alone, and to place their hope in him.

sens: Attraction, intense longing of one person for another
Powerful impulse or inclination, particularly that of sin
Inclination of the heart towards something or someone
H8669.detail:
1. Desire is a vivid and persistent attraction of one person for another. It is particularly the desire of a woman for a man: in Genesis 3:16, after sin, God tells the woman that her "desires" will be for her husband — she will seek him, she will be attracted to him. This is also the case in Song of Solomon 7:11, where the bride says that her beloved's desires are for her: he covets her, he desires her.

2. Desire can be a powerful and even threatening impulse, like that of sin itself. In Genesis 4:7, God warns Cain: "sin is crouching at the door, and its desires are for you" — sin lurks around Cain like a beast coveting its prey, wanting to devour him, to dominate him. It is a force that seeks to take possession of its target.

3. More broadly, desire is any inclination of the heart, any intense longing. It can be natural and good (that of a husband for his wife), or bad (that of sin which wants to enslave us). It is an inner force that drives us towards someone or something.
H8669.origine: This Hebrew word comes from a root that expresses the idea of seeking, running after, turning towards. The word literally designates what one turns towards with force, what one pursues. It describes the image of a physical and emotional attraction that pushes one to move towards the object of desire. It is a concrete and vivid word, painting the movement of desire.
H8669.emploi: This word appears three times in the Hebrew Bible. Twice it speaks of one person's desire for another: in Genesis 3:16, the woman's desire for her husband (a consequence of original sin), and in Song of Solomon 7:11, the beloved's desire for his friend (an image of joyful love). Once, in Genesis 4:7, it metaphorically designates the desire of sin itself which "crouches at the door" — a terrible image of sin personified as a beast wanting to devour its prey. The word thus changes context: from marital love to the threat of evil.
H8669.portee: This word reminds us that desire is a reality of the human heart, as old as sin. It can be good — the romantic attraction between husband and wife — or dangerous — the inclination of sin that seeks to dominate us. For the believer, this invites recognition of one's desires, examination of them, and asking God for the strength to refuse those that lead to evil, as Cain should have done.

sens: A gift, a donation offered to someone
An offering brought to a man of God or to an authority
H8670.detail: 1. A present is a gift given to someone to honor them or show respect. It is a material good given graciously. In 1 Samuel 9:7, Saul and his servant wonder what they can bring to Samuel as a present, for it is inappropriate to appear before a man of God empty-handed. 2. In this context, the present takes on a particular character: it is an offering due to one who holds a high status, particularly a prophet or a king. The absence of a present would be a sign of disrespect. The word thus designates both the ordinary gift and the offering of deference required by social and religious conventions.
H8670.origine: The Hebrew word תְּשׁוּרָה comes from a root that expresses the idea of seeing or looking (שׁור), with the prefix תּ which forms abstract nouns. The primary meaning evokes what is "looked at" or "noticed" by the one receiving it — that is, a gift worthy of attention, a present. This word belongs to a rich lexical field in biblical Hebrew for designating gifts, presents, and offerings according to their social or religious context.
H8670.emploi: This word appears only once in the Bible, in 1 Samuel 9:7. Saul, on his way with his servant to consult the prophet Samuel, realizes that he has nothing to offer him — neither provisions nor present. This unique occurrence emphasizes a well-established custom: before addressing a prophet or an important figure, one never appeared without a gift, big or small. This reflects the social importance of the present in ancient Israel as a mark of respect and humility.
H8670.portee: This passage teaches that approaching God or his representatives requires a heart disposition marked by respect and humility. Saul's concern not to appear without a present shows that a meeting with a man of God was not a trivial matter. Although the context is cultural and historical, it invites the believer to reflect on the importance of coming before God with a heart attentive to his majesty.

sens: Ordinal number designating the number 9 in a series or order
H8671.detail: 1. The word "ninth" simply designates the number 9 as a position in an ordered sequence. In 1 Chronicles 12:12, during the counting of the warriors who joined David, the "ninth" warrior named Elzabad is mentioned, placed after the eighth. It is a simple counting of ranks or stages. 2. The word is also used to refer to the ninth month of the Hebrew calendar (November-December), which regularly appears in historical and prophetic accounts. In Ezra 10:9, the people gather on the twentieth day of the "ninth" month to address a serious issue. This month often marks decisive moments in Israel's history, such as the beginning of the siege of Jerusalem in 2 Kings 25:1. 3. The word can also reference a cyclical period: in Leviticus 25:22, God promises that during the seventh year of rest for the land, the people will eat from the old harvest "until the ninth year," meaning until the new harvest arrives.
H8671.origine: The Hebrew word תְּשִׁיעִי comes from the root שׁעע (sh'a') or from the number nine (תְּשַׁע tisha'). It is a regularly formed ordinal adjective in Hebrew: the ninth in order. The family of Hebrew ordinals follows a pattern similar to Greek (first, second, third...), and this word belongs to the fundamental numeral series of the language.
H8671.emploi: The word appears 17 times in the Masoretic text, mainly to designate enumerated elements or specific periods. In lists of enumeration (lists of warriors, musicians, priestly families in 1 Chronicles), it simply indicates the ninth place. But it holds particular significance when it designates the ninth month of the Hebrew calendar: it then serves as a chronological marker rich in meaning in biblical history, especially during sieges or calamities (beginning of the siege of Jerusalem in 2 Kings 25:1, in Jeremiah 39:1, in Ezekiel 24:1). In Leviticus 25:22, it delineates a period of promised divine abundance during the cycle of seven years.
H8671.portee: For the reader, this word signals that God orders history and the periods of men according to precise and counted rhythms. The dates and the enumerations of "ninth" remind us that nothing happens by chance, neither misfortunes nor blessings: everything is inscribed in a calendar that God controls.

sens: Cardinal number equal to three times three
Ordinal number placed in ninth position
Number composed with other digits (like nineteen, one hundred nine)
H8672.detail:
1. The word designates the whole number nine, used to count objects or people. In Genesis 5:5, Adam lived nine hundred thirty years — the extreme age of the pre-flood patriarchs expressed with this number as a basis for calculation.
2. The word can also have an ordinal value (ninth), marking a position in a sequence or chronology. In 2 Kings 18:10, it reads "the ninth year of Hoshea": the ordinal word precisely situates a moment of reign in a series of years.
3. Finally, tescha is used in combination with other numbers to form composite figures. Genesis 11:25 shows Nahor living one hundred nineteen years: nine appears here as the last numeral element of an addition.
H8672.origine: The Hebrew word tescha comes from a simple root expressing the idea of the number nine. It is a fundamental number in the Hebrew numeral system, built on units of ten. The word is ancient, attested in all biblical texts, and is part of the basic vocabulary of counts, lists, and genealogies that structure the biblical narrative.
H8672.emploi: The word tescha appears 57 times in the Hebrew Bible, mainly in historical and legislative books. It is primarily used to express lifespans (genealogies in Genesis 5 and 11), periods of reign (2 Kings 14:2, 2 Kings 18:2, 2 Chronicles 29:1), military quantities (Judges 4:3: nine hundred iron chariots of Jabin), and cultic or territorial counts (Numbers 34:13: nine and a half tribes). In the division of Canaan (Joshua 13-19), the number nine regularly appears to count portions and cities. The historical-genealogical context largely dominates.
H8672.portee: This number, although purely quantitative, situates the reader in the precision of biblical facts. It reminds us that God presides over a measurable, countable history, the details of which are transmitted to us. The repetition of patriarchal lifespans with this number invites reflection on the mysterious length of pre-flood lives and on the unfolding of time according to the divine plan.

sens: The number 90, composed of nine tens
An advanced age, close to the end of life
H8673.detail:
1. Ninety is the number 90, formed of nine times ten. It mainly appears to count years of age or objects: Abram is ninety years old when God appears to him and promises him a descendant (Genesis 17:1), and Enosh fathers a son at that age (Genesis 5:9).
2. This number designates an exceptionally advanced age, a time when human life is nearing its end. Eli, the high priest, was ninety-eight years old and his eyes could no longer see (1 Samuel 4:15), showing how old age weakens the body. It is an age where only the grace of God can still give life, as when Abram fathers Isaac despite his old age.
H8673.origine: Tishim comes from the Hebrew root שׁעה (see ten), multiplied by nine. The word is simply composed: nine (teshaim) combined with ten (aseret). It is a round number, easy to count in biblical enumerations of genealogies, censuses, and Temple measurements.
H8673.emploi: This word appears 20 times in the Old Testament, mainly to give an age or count objects. It is found in genealogies (Genesis 5), with Abram when God miraculously rejuvenates him (Genesis 17), in accounts of elderly people (Eli in 1 Samuel 4), in lists of return from exile (Ezra and Nehemiah: families, cities, offerings), and in descriptions of the Temple (decorative pomegranates in Jeremiah 52:23, measurements in Ezekiel 41:12). The number emphasizes each time the importance of the moment: a great age, a large quantity, or a long symbolic period.
H8673.portee: Ninety reminds the reader that God acts even at the extreme limits of human life: Abram receives a promise and a descendant when everything seems impossible at the age of men. It is an invitation to trust in God beyond natural abilities. The number also evokes the wear of time and the weakness of our flesh, while witnessing to the vigor of Him who rejuvenates the hearts of believers.

sens: Persian governor of the region beyond the River at the time of the return from exile
Adversary of the reconstruction of the temple in Jerusalem
H8674.detail:
1. Thathnai is a historical figure, a Persian governor responsible for the region known as "beyond the River" (the Euphrates), during the time when the Jews returned from exile to begin rebuilding the temple in Jerusalem. He appears in Ezra 5:3 to question the workers about the authority that permitted them to build.

2. He initially opposes this reconstruction project and, along with his colleagues, sends a letter to King Darius to contest this undertaking (Ezra 5:6). However, after King Darius discovers the decree of Cyrus allowing this construction, Thathnai is ordered to cease his obstructions and support the work (Ezra 6:6, 6:13).
H8674.origine: The name Thathnai means "gift" or "present" in Persian. It is a title or personal name recorded in historical archives from the Achaemenid period, reflecting the presence of Persian authorities in the provinces of the empire.
H8674.emploi: Thathnai appears four times in the book of Ezra, with all passages directly concerning his role in the obstruction and then acceptance of the temple reconstruction (Ezra 5:3, 5:6, 6:6, 6:13). First, he questions the builders; then, he sends a formal letter to the king to contest the project; finally, after the royal intervention, he complies without resistance to Darius's decree. His story illustrates how God controls political events to accomplish His plans: an obstacle becomes an instrument of confirmation.
H8674.portee: The account of Thathnai shows that human opposition to God's plans, even when it comes from official powers, cannot prevent them. The Persian king, despite the opposition from his governor, ultimately supports the work of rebuilding the temple. This encourages believers to trust God even in the face of political or social obstacles.
